title: No public shame (Avot 3:11)
hook: Elazar of Modi'in: shaming someone in public costs a person dearly
tomorrow: how do you greet someone you'd rather avoid?

segments.voice: Two weeks of chapter three. This week: you and yours are his, the tree is torah too, review, deeds first, pleasant to people, and yesterday's line: don't waste the day.
screen: `DON'T WASTE THE DAY.` → `TWO WEEKS OF CHAPTER THREE.`

segments.voice: A speech, a microphone, a room full of friends, and one perfect joke at somebody's expense. Everyone laughs. One face goes pale. What costs more than money and takes one sentence? Rabbi Elazar of Modi'in lists grave things in Avot, and one of them is this: whoever shames his fellow in public. Even with Torah and good deeds, he says, that person has lost something no deed easily buys back.
screen: `ONE PERFECT JOKE.` → `ONE FACE GOES PALE.` → `WHOEVER SHAMES HIS FELLOW IN PUBLIC.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew is vivid: malbin p'nei chavero, whitening his fellow's face. The Talmud takes the picture literally. The red drains out and the white comes in, so shaming someone in public is like shedding blood. And it tells of Tamar, who, as she was being led out to be punished, would not name Judah in front of everyone; she sent him his own things privately and let him decide. Some sages draw the lesson that it's better to suffer than to shame someone in public. That's the day's word, lightly: no public shame. And it gathers the week. You and yours are His, so the person in front of you is His too. The tree is Torah too, and so is the face of the one you're about to joke about. Review: say it once more, and gentler. Deeds first: the kind act beats the clever line. Pleasant to people: let them rest around you. Don't waste the day on a laugh that costs someone their color.
screen: `WHITENING HIS FELLOW'S FACE.` · `TAMAR WOULD NOT NAME HIM.` · `NO PUBLIC SHAME.` · `THE WEEK, GATHERED.` · then, large: `NO PUBLIC SHAME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who's been the joke of the room lately, at work, at school, in a family chat. See the next time it starts, and find one plain sentence that would turn it gently, like, let's give them a break. Say that sentence once, under your breath, so it's ready.
No public shame: Elazar of Modi'in's warning, and the Talmud's picture of a face going white as the blood drains.
Your line: no public shame. Let every face in the room keep its own color. Two weeks, done.

howItsDone: Jewish ethics treats public embarrassment as a grave wrong; correction is meant to be private and gentle, and some communities give help to those in need discreetly so no one is shamed.

fork.setup: in a team meeting, a colleague's mistake is about to go up on the big screen in front of everyone. what does Avot 3:11 point to?
options: raise it with the colleague privately first.
show it; honesty means everyone should see.
say nothing ever; mistakes don't really matter.
fork.reveal: Tamar sent Judah his things privately rather than shame him in public. the mistake can still be fixed; the face doesn't have to go white.

It's fine if it's funny enough; a joke can't count as public shame.

chat.meaning: Avot 3:11 warns against whitening someone's face in public. Keep the laugh; aim it somewhere that costs nobody their color.

Elazar of Modi'in.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah; Avot 3:11 is his
